question: Why should you look farther ahead when driving doubles or triples than when driving a single vehicle?
choice_a: Because doubles and triples are not required to have brake lights on the rear trailer
choice_b: So you can read road signs before other drivers can see them
choice_c: So you can slow down and change lanes safely, since doubles and triples must be driven very smoothly to avoid rollover or jackknife
choice_d: Because the mirrors on a double or triple rig are smaller than on a single vehicle
explanation: The manual states doubles and triples must be driven very smoothly to avoid rollover or jackknife, so drivers should look farther ahead than in a single vehicle to slow down and change lanes safely.
source_note: Maryland Commercial Driver's License Manual (DL-151, 05/26), Maryland Department of Transportation Motor Vehicle Administration (MDOT MVA) -- Section 7, 7.1.4 Look Far Ahead

question: According to the manual, why do doubles and triples require more following distance and larger gaps than other commercial vehicles?
choice_a: They take up more space, are longer, and cannot be turned or stopped suddenly
choice_b: They have a lower center of gravity than single trailers
choice_c: Their brakes are more powerful than a single trailer's brakes
choice_d: They are exempt from all following-distance regulations
explanation: The manual explains doubles and triples take up more space than other commercial vehicles because they are longer and can't be turned or stopped suddenly, requiring more following distance and larger gaps when entering or crossing traffic.
source_note: Maryland Commercial Driver's License Manual (DL-151, 05/26), Maryland Department of Transportation Motor Vehicle Administration (MDOT MVA) -- Section 7, 7.1.5 Manage Space

question: Why must drivers be especially careful with doubles and triples in bad weather or on slippery roads?
choice_a: Their tires are always narrower than those on single trailers
choice_b: They are not equipped with any brakes on the rear trailer
choice_c: Federal law prohibits doubles and triples from using drive axles
choice_d: They have more length and more dead axles to pull with the drive axles, creating more chance for skids and loss of traction
explanation: The manual notes that in bad weather, slippery conditions, and mountain driving, doubles and triples drivers have more length and more dead axles to pull with their drive axles, meaning more chance for skids and loss of traction.
source_note: Maryland Commercial Driver's License Manual (DL-151, 05/26), Maryland Department of Transportation Motor Vehicle Administration (MDOT MVA) -- Section 7, 7.1.6 Bad Conditions

question: What should a driver keep in mind when choosing a parking spot for a vehicle pulling more than one trailer?
choice_a: Backing out is always easier for doubles and triples than for single trailers
choice_b: Always choose the spot closest to the building entrance regardless of layout
choice_c: Only parking spots with painted double lines are legal for doubles and triples
choice_d: Choose a spot that can be pulled straight through, since backing out of a spot takes a long time and is very difficult
explanation: The manual advises choosing a parking spot you can pull straight through because trying to back a doubles/triples rig out of a spot takes a lot of time and is very difficult.
source_note: Maryland Commercial Driver's License Manual (DL-151, 05/26), Maryland Department of Transportation Motor Vehicle Administration (MDOT MVA) -- Section 7, 7.1.7 Parking the Vehicle

question: Converter dollies built on or after what date must have antilock brakes, and how can you identify one?
choice_a: March 1, 1998; it will have a yellow lamp on the left side of the dolly
choice_b: January 1, 2000; it will have a red lamp on the rear of the dolly
choice_c: March 1, 1998; it will have a green lamp on the right side of the dolly
choice_d: January 1, 1998; it will have no visible identifying lamp
explanation: The manual states converter dollies built on or after March 1, 1998 must have antilock brakes, and these dollies will have a yellow lamp on the left side of the dolly.
source_note: Maryland Commercial Driver's License Manual (DL-151, 05/26), Maryland Department of Transportation Motor Vehicle Administration (MDOT MVA) -- Section 7, 7.1.8 Antilock Braking Systems on Converter Dollies

question: For the safest handling on the road, which trailer should be placed in the first position behind the tractor when coupling twin trailers?
choice_a: The more heavily loaded semi-trailer, with the lighter trailer in the rear
choice_b: It does not matter which trailer goes first as long as both are chocked
choice_c: Whichever trailer was loaded first, regardless of weight
choice_d: The lighter semi-trailer, with the heavier trailer in the rear
explanation: The manual states that for the safest handling on the road, the more heavily loaded semi-trailer should be in the first position behind the tractor, with the lighter trailer in the rear.
source_note: Maryland Commercial Driver's License Manual (DL-151, 05/26), Maryland Department of Transportation Motor Vehicle Administration (MDOT MVA) -- Section 7, 7.2.1 Coupling Twin Trailers

question: What is a converter dolly, as described in the manual?
choice_a: A type of brake chamber found only on triple-trailer combinations
choice_b: A hydraulic lift used exclusively for loading hazardous materials tanks
choice_c: A coupling device of one or two axles and a fifth wheel that couples a semi-trailer to the rear of a tractor-trailer combination, forming a double bottom rig
choice_d: A device used only to raise and lower the landing gear on a semi-trailer
explanation: The manual defines a converter dolly (converter gear) as a coupling device of one or two axles and a fifth wheel by which a semi-trailer can be coupled to the rear of a tractor-trailer combination, forming a double bottom rig.
source_note: Maryland Commercial Driver's License Manual (DL-151, 05/26), Maryland Department of Transportation Motor Vehicle Administration (MDOT MVA) -- Section 7, 7.2.1 Coupling Twin Trailers

question: When securing the second (rear) trailer before coupling, if it doesn't have spring brakes, what should you do to set the trailer's emergency brakes?
choice_a: Drive the tractor close to the trailer, connect the emergency line, charge the trailer air tank, then disconnect the emergency line
choice_b: Remove the trailer's wheels entirely until coupling is complete
choice_c: Leave the emergency line disconnected and rely solely on wheel chocks
choice_d: Charge the service line only, then disconnect the service line
explanation: The manual instructs that if the second trailer doesn't have spring brakes, you should drive the tractor close to the trailer, connect the emergency line, charge the trailer air tank, and disconnect the emergency line, which sets the trailer emergency brakes if slack adjusters are correctly adjusted.
source_note: Maryland Commercial Driver's License Manual (DL-151, 05/26), Maryland Department of Transportation Motor Vehicle Administration (MDOT MVA) -- Section 7, 7.2.1 Coupling Twin Trailers

question: Before backing a converter dolly under the rear trailer, what must be true about the trailer height?
choice_a: It must be slightly lower than the center of the fifth wheel, so the trailer is raised slightly when the dolly is pushed under
choice_b: It must be slightly higher than the center of the fifth wheel so the dolly slides in without contact
choice_c: Trailer height does not matter as long as the landing gear is fully raised
choice_d: It must be exactly level with the top of the dolly's tires
explanation: The manual states trailer height must be slightly lower than the center of the fifth wheel, so the trailer is raised slightly when the dolly is pushed under.
source_note: Maryland Commercial Driver's License Manual (DL-151, 05/26), Maryland Department of Transportation Motor Vehicle Administration (MDOT MVA) -- Section 7, 7.2.1 Connect Converter Dolly to Rear Trailer

question: What should you see when making a visual check of the coupling between the converter dolly and the rear trailer?
choice_a: A small gap between the upper and lower fifth wheel to allow for pivoting
choice_b: The safety chains completely disconnected until the vehicle is moving
choice_c: No space between the upper and lower fifth wheel, and locking jaws closed on the kingpin
choice_d: The locking jaws open around the kingpin for easy release
explanation: The manual specifies that during a visual check of coupling, there should not be space between the upper and lower fifth wheel, and the locking jaws should be closed on the kingpin.
source_note: Maryland Commercial Driver's License Manual (DL-151, 05/26), Maryland Department of Transportation Motor Vehicle Administration (MDOT MVA) -- Section 7, 7.2.1 Connect Converter Dolly to Rear Trailer

question: After coupling, how do you charge the trailer brakes and confirm air pressure has reached the rear of the second trailer?
choice_a: Charging trailer brakes is unnecessary once the pintle hook is locked
choice_b: Disconnect the service line and listen for silence, confirming no air is present
choice_c: Pull the 'air supply' knob out and listen at the front bumper of the tractor
choice_d: Push the 'air supply' knob in and check for air at the rear of the second trailer by opening the emergency line shut-off
explanation: The manual instructs to charge trailer brakes by pushing the 'air supply' knob in and checking for air at the rear of the second trailer by opening the emergency line shut-off; if air pressure isn't there, something is wrong and the brakes won't work.
source_note: Maryland Commercial Driver's License Manual (DL-151, 05/26), Maryland Department of Transportation Motor Vehicle Administration (MDOT MVA) -- Section 7, 7.2.1 Connect Converter Dolly to Rear Trailer

question: When uncoupling the rear trailer of a set of doubles, what is the first step listed in the manual?
choice_a: Disconnect the electrical cord before parking the rig
choice_b: Park the rig in a straight line on firm level ground and apply the parking brakes so the rig won't move
choice_c: Immediately release the pintle hook before parking
choice_d: Raise the landing gear of the second semi-trailer completely
explanation: The manual's uncoupling procedure begins with parking the rig in a straight line on firm level ground and applying the parking brakes so the rig won't move.
source_note: Maryland Commercial Driver's License Manual (DL-151, 05/26), Maryland Department of Transportation Motor Vehicle Administration (MDOT MVA) -- Section 7, 7.2.2 Uncoupling Twin Trailers

question: Why should you never unlock the pintle hook while the converter dolly is still under the rear trailer?
choice_a: The dolly tow bar may fly up, possibly causing injury and making it very difficult to re-couple
choice_b: It voids the manufacturer's warranty on the fifth wheel
choice_c: It causes the landing gear to collapse instantly
choice_d: It will automatically trigger the emergency brakes on the tractor
explanation: The manual warns never to unlock the pintle hook with the dolly still under the rear trailer because the dolly tow bar may fly up, possibly causing injury and making it very difficult to re-couple.
source_note: Maryland Commercial Driver's License Manual (DL-151, 05/26), Maryland Department of Transportation Motor Vehicle Administration (MDOT MVA) -- Section 7, 7.2.2 Uncouple Converter Dolly

question: When uncoupling a triple-trailer rig, what is done first?
choice_a: Uncouple the third trailer by pulling the dolly out, then unhitching the dolly using the method for uncoupling doubles
choice_b: Uncouple the tractor from the first trailer before touching the rear trailers
choice_c: Uncouple the first trailer from the tractor, then work backward
choice_d: Remove all safety chains from every trailer simultaneously
explanation: The manual states that to uncouple a triple-trailer rig, you first uncouple the third trailer by pulling the dolly out and unhitching it using the method for uncoupling doubles, then uncouple the remainder of the rig as you would any double-bottom rig.
source_note: Maryland Commercial Driver's License Manual (DL-151, 05/26), Maryland Department of Transportation Motor Vehicle Administration (MDOT MVA) -- Section 7, 7.2.3 Coupling and Uncoupling Triple Trailers

question: When inspecting the lower fifth wheel on a doubles or triples combination, what should you check besides secure mounting to the frame?
choice_a: That the fifth wheel has been replaced within the last year
choice_b: That the fifth wheel matches the trailer manufacturer exactly
choice_c: That there are no missing or damaged parts and there is enough grease
choice_d: That the fifth wheel is painted a bright color for visibility
explanation: The manual's coupling system inspection checklist for the lower fifth wheel includes making sure it is securely mounted to the frame, has no missing or damaged parts, and has enough grease.
source_note: Maryland Commercial Driver's License Manual (DL-151, 05/26), Maryland Department of Transportation Motor Vehicle Administration (MDOT MVA) -- Section 7, 7.3.1 Additional Checks - Coupling System Areas

question: When inspecting a set of double or triple trailers, what position should the shut-off valve be in at the rear of the front trailer(s) versus the rear of the last trailer?
choice_a: Both should always be CLOSED regardless of position
choice_b: Both should always be OPEN regardless of position
choice_c: Rear of front trailers should be OPEN; rear of the last trailer should be CLOSED
choice_d: Rear of front trailers should be CLOSED; rear of the last trailer should be OPEN
explanation: The manual's inspection checklist states the rear shut-off valve of front trailers should be OPEN, while the rear shut-off valve of the last trailer should be CLOSED.
source_note: Maryland Commercial Driver's License Manual (DL-151, 05/26), Maryland Department of Transportation Motor Vehicle Administration (MDOT MVA) -- Section 7, 7.3.1 Additional Checks - Double and Triple Trailers

question: Which of the following is part of the landing gear inspection for doubles and triples?
choice_a: Check that it is fully raised, no parts are missing, and it is not bent or damaged
choice_b: Check that the landing gear is painted to match the trailer color
choice_c: Check that the landing gear is lowered fully at all times during transport
choice_d: Check that the landing gear crank handle has been removed and stored separately
explanation: The manual's landing gear inspection checklist requires checking that it is fully raised, that no parts are missing, and that it is not bent or damaged, along with the crank handle being in place and secured.
source_note: Maryland Commercial Driver's License Manual (DL-151, 05/26), Maryland Department of Transportation Motor Vehicle Administration (MDOT MVA) -- Section 7, 7.3.1 Additional Checks - Landing Gear

question: How do you check that air flows all the way to the rear of a set of double or triple trailers?
choice_a: Apply the parking brake and immediately drive away to test brake response
choice_b: Check only the tractor's own air tank pressure gauge
choice_c: Disconnect the tractor from all trailers and listen at the fifth wheel
choice_d: Push in the red 'trailer air supply' knob, go to the rear, and open the emergency line shut-off valve at the rear of the last trailer to listen for escaping air
explanation: The manual describes pushing in the red 'trailer air supply' knob, going to the rear of the rig, and opening the emergency line shut-off valve at the rear of the last trailer; hearing air escape shows the entire system is charged.
source_note: Maryland Commercial Driver's License Manual (DL-151, 05/26), Maryland Department of Transportation Motor Vehicle Administration (MDOT MVA) -- Section 7, 7.4.1 Additional Air Brake Checks - Check That Air Flows to All Trailers

question: When testing the tractor protection valve, the trailer air supply control should pop out to the 'emergency' position when air pressure falls into what range, according to the manual?
choice_a: Usually within the range of 100 to 120 psi
choice_b: Usually within the range of 60 to 90 psi
choice_c: Usually within the range of 20 to 45 psi
choice_d: Usually within the range of 5 to 10 psi
explanation: The manual states the trailer air supply control (tractor protection valve control) should pop out or move to 'emergency' when air pressure falls into the manufacturer-specified range, usually 20 to 45 psi.
source_note: Maryland Commercial Driver's License Manual (DL-151, 05/26), Maryland Department of Transportation Motor Vehicle Administration (MDOT MVA) -- Section 7, 7.4.1 Additional Air Brake Checks - Test Tractor Protection Valve

question: What could happen if the tractor protection valve does not work properly?
choice_a: The trailer's lights would fail to illuminate at night
choice_b: An air hose or trailer brake leak could drain all the air from the tractor, causing the emergency brakes to come on with possible loss of control
choice_c: The fifth wheel would automatically release from the kingpin
choice_d: The landing gear would lower automatically while driving
explanation: The manual warns that if the tractor protection valve doesn't work properly, an air hose or trailer brake leak could drain all the air from the tractor, causing the emergency brakes to come on with possible loss of control.
source_note: Maryland Commercial Driver's License Manual (DL-151, 05/26), Maryland Department of Transportation Motor Vehicle Administration (MDOT MVA) -- Section 7, 7.4.1 Additional Air Brake Checks - Test Tractor Protection Valve

question: How should trailer service brakes be tested, and how are they normally applied during operation?
choice_a: Tested by removing the wheels of the last trailer
choice_b: Tested only with the foot pedal, and never with a hand valve
choice_c: Tested with the hand valve (trolley valve), but controlled in normal operation with the foot pedal, which applies air to the service brakes at all wheels
choice_d: Tested by disconnecting the emergency line and observing trailer roll
explanation: The manual explains trailer brakes should be tested with the hand valve, but controlled in normal operation with the foot pedal, which applies air to the service brakes at all wheels.
source_note: Maryland Commercial Driver's License Manual (DL-151, 05/26), Maryland Department of Transportation Motor Vehicle Administration (MDOT MVA) -- Section 7, 7.4.1 Additional Air Brake Checks - Test Trailer Service Brakes
